newsitem.title: ITALY: Food summit opens with Zaire plea, pledge on hunger.
newsitem.headline: Food summit opens with Zaire plea, pledge on hunger.

text.p: A U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit opened on Wednesday in the shadow of starvation in Zaire and to appeals from Pope John Paul and other leaders to end what one called hunger's "affront to all of humanity".
The first summit on the fight for food began amid suffering facing more than one million ethnic Hutu refugees caught at the centre of warfare in eastern Zaire.

The crisis is not on the official agenda but the immediate tragedy clearly weighed on the gathering, which opened with leaders adopting an ambitious plan to feed more than 400 million additional mouths by the year 2015.

"For the tribes and ethnic groups who are killing each other, hunger and famine are, in the final analysis, weapons of war to be used to kill and kill again," U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali said in an impassioned plea on the Zaire crisis.
"It is this terrible reality which we must keep in mind to understand how and why we have to act.

"From this platform, in this Eternal City, I make a solemn appeal to peoples and to states to take part, all of them, in the collective action we will undertake in the Great Lakes region," Boutros-Ghali said.
"It is by our ability to take charge of this tragedy in a collective, concerted fashion that we will give a real meaning to human solidarity," he told the 194-nation, five-day summit.

The summit, held by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation at its Fascist-era Rome headquarters amid blanket security, is set to receive more than 80 heads of state and government over its five days, according to FAO.

They are expected to include veteran communist Cuban leader Fidel Castro, who was given a prominent role on Wednesday when he was appointed one of six summit vice-chairmen. Castro is not scheduled to arrive until Friday, diplomatic sources say.
The keynote documents, a Declaration on World Food Security and a Plan of Action to provide food for all, were agreed in advance and adopted by acclamation at the first session.
They contain a specific pledge to halve the number of people facing chronic hunger and malnutrition -- 840 million or nearly 14 percent of the planet's population -- no later than 2015.

Pope John Paul challenged heads of state and delegates to make every effort to "eliminate the spectre of hunger from the planet" or face the consequences, saying it was unacceptable that some people starved while others "lived in opulence".
A strict opponent of contraception, the 76-year-old Roman Catholic leader also swiped at development experts who say population control is the answer to ending food scarcity.
"It would be illusory to believe that an arbitrary stabilisation of the world population, or even its reduction, could solve the problem of hunger directly," the Pope said.
He called for a distribution of wealth and food "based not only on profit" and urged rich countries to cut arms spending and remove the burden of foreign debt on poor nations.
"This contrast between poverty and wealth is intolerable for humanity," the Pontiff told delegates.

He was echoed by several other speakers including Boutros-Ghali, who said: "It is quite intolerable to see certain countries wasting or destroying food whereas others cannot provide their children with even elementary needs."
Edwin Carrington, Secretary-General of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), said hunger was a sign of a failure of political will.
"This situation is an affront to all of humanity and a condemnation of our collective leadership," he said.
A ministerial World Food Conference in 1974 pledged to end hunger within a decade and FAO says the new target is both more reasonable and more achievable.

FAO's Senegalese director general Jacques Diouf, addressing scepticism that the summit aims may again remain empty words, told the meeting governments had to take action when they went home to avoid the risk of their commitments "turning sour".

Clearly vexed, he said FAO's budget amounted to "less than what nine developed countries spend on dog and cat food in six days and, listen to me, less than five percent of what the inhabitants of one developed country spend each year on slimming products to counter the effects of over-eating."
